newsitem.title: USA: Fixing Medicaid tops Louisiana Gov's budget plan.
newsitem.headline: Fixing Medicaid tops Louisiana Gov's budget plan.

text.p: Louisiana Gov. Mike Foster said ending the state's reliance on federal Medicaid bailouts would be his top budget priority during the upcoming spring legislative session.
He outlined his budget priorities late Thursday after announcing he would postpone a special legislative session on sales taxes until after the regular spring session, which begins March 31.

The governor had previously planned to call a Feb 23 special session to address the renewal of a one-cent sales tax that brings in $110 million annually and will expire June 30. His original proposal called for using all $110 million for educational improvements.
His new proposal still calls for renewal of the sales tax, with $75 million earmarked for public schools and $35 million to be directed to a permanent Medicaid solution.
The state has relied on federal Medicaid bailouts to balance its budget, under a program that alloted extra funds for states with a disproportionate share of poor people.
"That time is at an end. We have got to pay the piper," Foster said.

Federal officials have already told the state it was unlikely Congress would approve a bailout this year by allowing Louisiana to contribute anything less than the 30 percent match it was scheduled to start making in fiscal 1998.

That was partly because an increasing number of states have asked for help, and partly because Louisiana will have a surplus for fiscal 1997. Last month, the state revenue estimating conference said state would have $228 more than previously expected, which is to be allocated by the legislature in a supplemental spending bill.
If the state does get a federal bailout this year, it would have to increase its total Medicaid program to $3.6 billion, because of the mandates that come with the extra money, Foster said.
"This would simply have compounded our problem next year and in the following years," he said.
His new plan would allocate $3.19 billion for Medicaid in fiscal 1998 and increaes the state's matching level to $950 million, the level it would have been required to reach three years from now.
Foster said that would keep Medicaid at an affordable level, freeing up future revenues for economic growth for education and infrastrcture investments.
"This would bring us to a point where there would be no Medicaid holes in future years. We would be just like all other states. No crises. No fiscal instability," Foster said.

His plan would use some of the surplus, plus $35 million of the renewed one-cent sales tax to make the higher Medicaid match. It would also prepay some long-term debt with surplus funds, freeing up $26 million in recurring revenues.
Foster is expected to release his complete budget in a couple of weeks, but he said it would still include new spending for education.

Public education would get an additional $103 million to buy computers and science equipment, establish a revolivng loan fund for start-up charter schools and award bonuses to schools that meet certain standards.
Higher education would get an additional $52.6 million, with $30 million of that earmarked for postponed maintenance of college and university buildings, and $10 million for equipment purchases.
